title: Maker's Workshop: Sort Your Supplies
description: Welcome to the Maker's Workshop! Sort 20 craft and DIY materials into the correct project categories -- Woodworking, Electronics, Textiles, and Papercraft. Learn what each material does and which projects use them!
theme: Crafting, DIY, Maker Movement & Hands-On Learning
learning_objectives: Identify common crafting materials and their uses
Understand the four major DIY categories: Woodworking, Electronics, Textiles, Papercraft
Learn about tools and techniques used in hands-on making
Develop material selection skills for real-world projects
Explore the maker movement and hands-on STEM learning

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Read the name and description of each material card
Drag the card to the correct project category: Woodworking, Electronics, Textiles, or Papercraft
Earn points for correct placements -- lose points for wrong ones
Double-click any card for fun facts about the material
Sort all 20 materials to complete the workshop!
tips: Think about what each material is made of -- wood, metal, fabric, or paper?
Some materials might seem tricky -- a soldering iron uses metal but belongs in Electronics!
If unsure, read the description carefully for clues about the project type

buckets.label: Woodworking
buckets.description: Tools and materials for building with wood

buckets.label: Electronics
buckets.description: Components and tools for electrical projects

items.label: Sandpaper (120 Grit)
items.description: Abrasive paper used to smooth rough wooden surfaces before painting or varnishing.
items.details: Sandpaper comes in different grit numbers. Lower numbers (60-80) are coarse for removing material quickly. Higher numbers (220-400) are fine for smooth finishing. The grit refers to the number of abrasive particles per square inch.
items.fun_fact: The first sandpaper was made in China in the 13th century using crushed shells and seeds glued to parchment!

items.label: LED Strip (WS2812B)
items.description: A strip of individually addressable RGB LEDs that can display any colour and pattern.
items.details: WS2812B LED strips have tiny microchips built into each LED, allowing you to control each one independently using just one data wire. They run on 5V and can create rainbow effects, animations, and respond to music.
items.fun_fact: A single WS2812B LED strip of 60 LEDs can produce over 16 million colour combinations per LED!

items.label: Felt Fabric Sheet
items.description: A soft, non-woven fabric made from pressed fibres, perfect for soft toys, decorations, and appliques.
items.details: Felt doesn't fray when cut, making it ideal for beginners. It's made by compressing and matting fibres together using heat, moisture, and pressure. It's one of the oldest known textiles, predating weaving!
items.fun_fact: According to legend, felt was discovered by Saint Clement, who put wool in his shoes for comfort and found it had turned into felt from the pressure and moisture!

items.label: A4 Cardstock (300 GSM)
items.description: Thick, sturdy paper used for greeting cards, model building, and pop-up structures.
items.details: GSM stands for Grams per Square Metre -- regular printer paper is 80 GSM while cardstock ranges from 200-350 GSM. The higher the GSM, the thicker and sturdier the paper.
items.fun_fact: The world's largest paper airplane, made from cardstock-like material, had a wingspan of 18 metres and flew 64 metres!

items.label: Wood Glue (PVA)
items.description: A strong adhesive specifically formulated for bonding wood pieces together in joinery.
items.details: PVA (Polyvinyl Acetate) wood glue creates bonds stronger than the wood itself when properly clamped. It dries clear, is non-toxic, and cleans up with water. It needs 30-60 minutes of clamping and 24 hours for full cure.
items.fun_fact: A properly glued wood joint is actually stronger than a nailed one -- the glue bonds at a molecular level!

items.label: Solderless Breadboard
items.description: A plastic board with holes for prototyping electronic circuits without soldering.
items.details: Breadboards have internal metal strips that connect holes in rows. The two long strips on each side are power rails (+/-). Components are plugged in and connected with jumper wires. Perfect for testing circuits before soldering.
items.fun_fact: In the early days of electronics, people literally built circuits on wooden bread-cutting boards -- that's how the name stuck!

items.label: Embroidery Hoop (6 inch)
items.description: A circular frame that holds fabric taut while you stitch embroidery designs.
items.details: Embroidery hoops come in bamboo, wood, or plastic. The inner hoop goes under the fabric, the outer hoop tightens over it with a screw mechanism. Keeping fabric taut ensures even, neat stitches.
items.fun_fact: Embroidery is one of the oldest arts -- samples have been found in ancient Egypt dating back to 3000 BC!

items.label: Origami Paper (15cm x 15cm)
items.description: Thin, colourful paper sheets specially sized for the Japanese art of paper folding.
items.details: Traditional origami paper (kami) is coloured on one side and white on the other. Standard size is 15cm x 15cm. Traditional origami uses a single sheet with no cutting or gluing -- only folding!
items.fun_fact: The world record for smallest origami crane was folded from a 1mm x 1mm piece of paper using a microscope and tweezers!

items.label: Wood Chisel (12mm)
items.description: A sharp-edged hand tool for carving, shaping, and cutting wood joints.
items.details: Chisels come in different widths for different tasks. They're used with a mallet for heavy cutting or by hand for fine detail work. Keeping the blade razor-sharp is essential for clean cuts.
items.fun_fact: Ancient Egyptian carpenters used copper chisels to build the wooden boats buried in the Great Pyramids over 4,500 years ago!

items.label: Resistor Assortment Kit
items.description: A collection of resistors in various values, used to control current flow in circuits.
items.details: Resistors have coloured bands that indicate their resistance value in ohms. The colour code follows a specific pattern: Black=0, Brown=1, Red=2, Orange=3, Yellow=4, Green=5, Blue=6, Violet=7, Grey=8, White=9.
items.fun_fact: Students remember resistor colours with the mnemonic: 'BB ROY of Great Britain has a Very Good Wife' (Black, Brown, Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Violet, Grey, White)!

items.label: Cotton Embroidery Thread
items.description: Six-strand divisible thread used for cross-stitch, embroidery, and decorative stitching.
items.details: DMC embroidery thread comes in over 500 colours. Each length has 6 strands that can be separated -- use 2 strands for delicate work, all 6 for bold designs. Cotton thread is colourfast and can be washed.
items.fun_fact: The Bayeux Tapestry, which is actually an embroidered cloth depicting the Norman Conquest of England (1066 AD), is 70 metres long!

items.label: Crepe Paper Rolls
items.description: Textured, stretchy paper used for making paper flowers, streamers, and decorations.
items.details: Crepe paper gets its wrinkled texture from a process called 'creping' -- the paper is pressed against a blade while wet, creating tiny folds. It can stretch up to 200% of its original length.
items.fun_fact: Crepe paper flowers are a traditional craft in Mexico called 'flores de papel' and are used to decorate altars during Day of the Dead celebrations!

items.label: Bar Clamps (Set of 2)
items.description: Adjustable clamps used to hold glued wood pieces together while the adhesive cures.
items.details: The golden rule of woodworking: you can never have too many clamps! Bar clamps apply even pressure along their length. Apply enough pressure to squeeze out excess glue but not so much that you deform the wood.
items.fun_fact: Professional woodworkers often own 50+ clamps -- there's even a saying: 'The number of clamps you need is the number you have, plus one more!'

items.label: Arduino Nano
items.description: A tiny, programmable microcontroller board perfect for small electronic projects and wearables.
items.details: The Arduino Nano has 22 digital pins and 8 analog pins, runs at 16 MHz, and can be programmed in C/C++. It's smaller than a AA battery but can control LEDs, motors, sensors, and displays.
items.fun_fact: Arduino was created in 2005 by a team in Italy. The name comes from a bar in Ivrea, Italy, which was named after King Arduino of Italy (1002 AD)!

items.label: Sewing Pins & Pincushion
items.description: Thin, sharp pins used to temporarily hold fabric pieces together before sewing.
items.details: Glass-head pins are heat-resistant and won't melt under an iron. Ball-point pins are designed for knit fabrics to avoid snagging. The pincushion often contains an emery bag to keep pins sharp.
items.fun_fact: In medieval England, pins were so expensive that 'pin money' became a term for a wife's personal spending allowance -- and the term is still used today!

items.label: Paper Quilling Strips
items.description: Thin paper strips (3-5mm wide) rolled into coils and shaped for decorative paper art.
items.details: Quilling involves rolling, shaping, and gluing thin paper strips into intricate designs. Basic shapes include tight coils, loose coils, teardrops, and marquise shapes. These combine to create flowers, animals, and abstract patterns.
items.fun_fact: Quilling was practiced by Renaissance nuns and monks who rolled gilded paper strips salvaged from book edges to decorate religious texts!

items.label: Wooden Dowel Rods
items.description: Cylindrical wooden sticks used for joinery, model building, and structural support in projects.
items.details: Dowels are used in woodworking joints as an alternative to screws -- holes are drilled in both pieces, dowels are glued in, and the pieces are clamped together. Common sizes range from 6mm to 12mm diameter.
items.fun_fact: IKEA furniture uses more wooden dowels than any other company in the world -- they go through billions of dowels per year!

items.label: Digital Multimeter
items.description: A measuring instrument that checks voltage, current, and resistance in electrical circuits.
items.details: A multimeter is the most essential tool in electronics. It measures AC/DC voltage, current, resistance, and often includes a continuity tester (beeps when circuit is complete). Learning to use one is the first step in electronics.
items.fun_fact: The first multimeter was invented in 1920 by Donald Macadie, a British Post Office engineer, and was called an Avometer (Amps, Volts, Ohms)!

items.label: Fabric Scissors (Dressmaking Shears)
items.description: Sharp, angled scissors designed specifically for cutting fabric cleanly without fraying.
items.details: Fabric scissors have longer blades than regular scissors, with one blade slightly angled for cutting fabric flat on a table. NEVER use fabric scissors on paper -- it dulls the blade and ruins the scissor's ability to cut fabric cleanly.
items.fun_fact: The world's most expensive scissors are Japanese 'Hasami' by Sasuke Cutlery, hand-forged from tamahagane steel (same as samurai swords) and cost over Rs 50,000!

items.label: Decoupage Paper & Mod Podge
items.description: Decorative printed tissue paper and adhesive sealant for covering surfaces with paper art.
items.details: Decoupage (from French 'decouper' meaning 'to cut') involves cutting out paper designs and gluing them onto objects like boxes, trays, and furniture. Mod Podge acts as both glue and sealant, creating a smooth, durable finish.
items.fun_fact: Decoupage was so popular in 18th-century Venice that it was called 'lacca povera' (poor man's lacquer) because it let ordinary people decorate furniture to look like expensive hand-painted pieces!

glossary_terms.definition: The mental effort required to process information and make decisions.
glossary_terms.example: Having too many options at once makes decisions harder and slower.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Working memory has limits. Experts chunk information into patterns, reducing cognitive load and enabling faster decisions.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Experienced doctors diagnose faster not because they think harder, but because they recognize patterns instantly.

glossary_terms.definition: Identifying recurring structures or relationships in information.
glossary_terms.example: Noticing that certain question types always have two plausible answers helps you focus faster.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Pattern recognition is a core skill in chess, medicine, engineering, and sport. It develops through deliberate practice.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Air traffic controllers recognize dangerous flight patterns faster than computers because of years of pattern training.

glossary_terms.definition: The ability to direct mental attention toward what matters most and ignore distractions.
glossary_terms.example: Under time pressure, completing questions you're confident about before tackling harder ones.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Focus is a trainable skill. The Pomodoro method, mindfulness, and deliberate practice all improve sustained attention.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Olympic athletes train mental focus as rigorously as physical skills — pressure performance depends on it.

coaching_moment: If you get something wrong, reset and continue. Resilience isn't about never failing — it's about how quickly you get back on track.
cultural_context: Focused micro-skill practice builds the cognitive foundations for complex performance. Maker's Workshop: Sort Your Supplies provides the targeted repetition that supplements India's formal curriculum with actionable, measurable skill development.
reflection_prompt: What pattern did you start to recognize as you played? How will you use it next time?
